svg.title: Default deny is a one-line rule; the whitelist behind it is a permanent operating cost with four questions and three failure modes
svg.desc: Three panels. Left, the easy half: default deny is written once - a deny-all rule plus explicit permits - and it takes one afternoon. Middle, the hard half, four governance questions nobody puts in the design document: who submits a request, who approves it and against what business justification, how many minutes until the permit is live when the business is down, and who removes the rule when the project that needed it ends. Right, three failure modes when no owner exists: the list only grows, so after eighteen months it is a flat network with paperwork; the emergency bypass becomes the permanent path; and after a staff change nobody dares delete a rule because nobody knows what it protects. Bottom band: four patterns that make the whitelist survivable - a request portal so the ticket is the policy, expiry dates on every permit, a monthly diff review that names stale rules, and one documented emergency path with a timer and an owner.
svg.text: Truth #4: the deny-all rule is one afternoon; the whitelist is an operating cost forever
The design document ends at "default deny". The network does not - every permitted flow has an owner, a reason, an expiry and a reviewer
THE EASY HALF · WRITTEN ONCE
What the standard says
deny ip any any ! the default
permit tcp 10.1.0.0/16 host 10.9.9.9 eq 443
one line, reviewed once, copied to twenty devices
Effort: one afternoon · Owner: whoever wrote it ·
Change rate: near zero · Risk: near zero
This half is a configuration task. It can be
finished, signed off and forgotten - which is
exactly why it is the half people design.
THE HARD HALF · RUN FOREVER
Four questions the design doc never asks

g.text: The application owner, in writing - not a phone call
A named approver with a business justification - and a
security reviewer who can say no and be backed
How long until it is live?
A number, in minutes. If the answer is "two weeks", the
shadow path through the old firewall is already built
Someone, on a date. "Temporary" without an expiry is a
permanent rule with a reassuring label

svg.text: WHEN NOBODY OWNS IT
Three failure modes, all observed
1 · The list only grows
18 months later the "segmented" network has 40 any-any
rules - it is a flat network wearing paperwork
2 · The bypass becomes the path
The emergency rule opened during an incident is never
removed, so the design's real policy is the bypass
3 · Nobody dares delete
After a staff change every rule is "possibly needed",
so the audit produces a list, not a decision
FOUR PATTERNS THAT MAKE THE WHITELIST SURVIVABLE

g.text: The ticket is the policy object:
ask one question per new rule
in 4 hours, and the on-call has to
open a review ticket when it fires

svg.text: Design question to put in the document:
"Who is the owner of the whitelist, and what is the median time from request to permitted flow?"
If the design has no name and no number here, the segmentation exists on the diagram only - the operational network will route around it.
